sections.body:
[Stub: this library does not hold the text of Part IV. This section lists what the print holds, from the Guide's Contents, with a few sentences and the two figures of pp. IV-3 to IV-6 as printed. For the rest, consult the printed Guide.]

Part IV, Mechanistic-Empirical Design Procedures (pp. IV-3 to IV-11), holds (Contents): 1.1 Introduction (p. IV-3); 1.2 Benefits (p. IV-4); 1.3 Framework for Development and Application (p. IV-4); 1.4 Implementation (p. IV-7): 1.4.1 Design Considerations, 1.4.2 Input Data, 1.4.3 Equipment Acquisition, 1.4.4 Computer Hardware and Software, 1.4.5 Training Personnel, 1.4.6 Field Testing and Calibration, 1.4.7 Testing; 1.5 Summary (p. IV-10); References for Part IV (p. IV-11).

[p. IV-3] Part IV of the Guide is a brief overview of the use of analytical and mechanistic procedures for the design and evaluation of pavement structures.

A state of the knowledge summary of mechanistic design procedures has been prepared as a working document and can be found in Volume 3 of the Guide. Volume 3 contains nine chapters and an appendix which describe in detail the current status of the development and use of these procedures for design of new and rehabilitated pavements.

The design methodology incorporated in the 1972 issue of the AASHTO Design Guide for flexible pavements did not incorporate mechanistic procedures, although the supporting work, included in NCHRP Report 128 (14), did introduce such concepts for possible future use in the Guide. This issue (1986) of the [p. IV-4] Guide has indirectly used mechanistic procedures for evaluating seasonal damage and to establish coefficients for drainage and load transfer. Also, the use of the resilient modulus to represent material properties introduces the concept that paving materials can be represented by a quasi-elastic modulus.

[Note: "This issue (1986)" is printed so in the 1993 Guide (pp. IV-3 to IV-4).]

The primary benefits which could accrue from the successful application of mechanistic procedures will be: (1) improved reliability for design, (2) ability to predict specific types of distress, and (3) the ability to extrapolate from limited field and laboratory results.

Figure 1.1 illustrates the framework for the development of mechanistic-empirical design procedures for new designs and for rehabilitation. Figure 1.2 illustrates the application to an overlay for flexible pavements.

[Figure 1.1. Example Approach for the Development of a Mechanistic-Empirical Design Model (p. IV-5): a flow chart in two parts. Initial Design Development Methodology: Traffic, Subgrade Properties, Environment and Pavement Material Characteristics (with Aging, Uncertainty and Construction Requirements) lead to Trial Pavement Thicknesses, Structural Analysis (Note: Stress, Strain or Deformation Analysis) and Distress Analysis for Fatigue Cracking, Rutting, Thermal Cracking, Frost Effects, Reflection Cracking, Faulting, Punchout, Roughness, Volume Change Effects and Others; then, with Limiting Values of Distress and Reliability (Safety Factor), to Calibrated Distress Predictions, Life Cycle Prediction and Life Cycle Costs (Economic Analysis: Initial Cost, Maintenance Cost, User Cost, Salvage Value, Discount Rate). Rehabilitation Methodology: Traffic, Inputs (see above for initial design), NDT and Condition Survey lead to Rehabilitated Pavements (with Alternative Treatments, Note: Including Do Nothing), Structural Analysis, Distress Analysis over the Modes of Distress from Fatigue Cracking to Roughness, Calibrated Distress Criteria with Reliability (Safety Factor), Life Cycle Prediction, Economic Analysis and Life Cycle Cost.]

[Figure 1.2. Overlay Design Procedure Using Elastic Layered Theory to Represent Pavement Response (p. IV-6): a flow chart. Condition Surveys and Non Destructive Testing (Deflection, Curvature etc.) lead to Analysis Sections, Sampling/Testing and Materials Characterization, then Compute Deflections, Curvature, etc., and Compare: Not Acceptable returns to Adjust Material Properties; Accept goes on to Adjust Material Properties (Seasonal Effects, Load) and Compute Distress Determinants. Fatigue (Unit Damage) and Rutting (Unit Deformation) with Traffic give the Remaining Life, compared to choose No Overlay or Overlay Trial Sections; for the overlay trial sections, Compute Distress Determinants, then Fatigue (Unit Damage) and Rutting (Unit Deformation) with Traffic are compared on a small chart.]
